newsitem.title: IRAQ: KDP rebels bar reporters from entering Arbil.
newsitem.headline: KDP rebels bar reporters from entering Arbil.

text.p: Rebels of the pro- Baghdad Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) banned a group of Western reporters on an Iraqi government-sponsored trip from entering the Kurdish city of Arbil on Sunday.

KDP guerrillas with assault rifles and hand grenades fastened to their belts at a checkpoint close to Qarzalah, seven km (four miles) west of Arbil, ordered the reporters back, along with their Iraqi guides.

Qarzala, once a booming agricultural village, was deserted and then ruined during the past two years of fighting between the KDP and their rival militia of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) of Jalal Talabani.
KDP's leader Barzani ousted the PUK from Arbil in a joint assault with Iraqi armoured troops on the city on August 31 and is now Iraqi Kurdistan's only strongman.
The buses carrying Western reporters had passed three KDP checkpoints on the 90 km (56 miles) highway from Mosul to Arbil but were not allowed into the city by Kurdish rebels guarding its outskirts.
Otherwise, the two-lane highway was busy with trucks and cars moving in both directions. Arbil is about 350 km (218 miles) north of Baghdad.
The reporters were prevented from taking pictures or conducting interviews.
The rebels were busy decorating their checkpoints once manned by PUK rebels with their flags and pictures of their leader Masoud Barzani, removing all signs of their rival.
Iraq's move on Arbil prompted U.S. President Bill Clinton to order American forces to fire 44 cruise missiles against Iraqi air defences in the south.

Along the road, convoys of trucks loaded with locally produced vegetables such as potatoes, onions and apples along with other commodites smuggled from Iran or Turkey, were heading toward Mosul, Iraq's second largest city. Arbil is also linked with a highway direct to Baghdad and traders said it was also open to traffic.
Fuel trucks from Mosul went through without interruption. President Saddam Hussein last week decided to remove all restrictions on the movement of trade and people to the area.

Information ministry guides did not say why the rebels did not want the journalists to enter Arbil. Local reporters representing state-run newspapers and a couple of other Iraqi journalists employed by Western news agencies, travelling on their own, said they had no problem entering the city.
Iraqi checkpoints on the highway to Mosul were about 50 km (30 miles) west of Arbil. There was no sign of Iraqi military presence in the portion of the road under KDP guerrillas.
